facts.raw_span: A 62-year-old woman with multiple sclerosis
treated with fingolimod for 3 years
tender nodule on her forehead, which had gradually grown over 3 weeks
bumping her forehead on an air-conditioning unit several months prior
denied fever, neck stiffness, and photophobia
Eroded, crusted papule on the left forehead
No other lesions on full-body skin examination
White blood cell count: 3.9/μL
Lymphocyte count: 0.65/μL
Skin biopsy: Granulomatous inflammation composed of histiocytes, giant cells, and lymphocytes admixed with numerous narrow-budding yeasts with thick capsules
Tissue culture: Grew Cryptococcus neoformans
HIV test: Negative

Lymphocyte count: 0.65/μL

Tissue culture: Grew Cryptococcus neoformans
HIV test: Negative

concepts.why: The skin biopsy showed granulomatous inflammation with numerous narrow-budding yeasts with thick capsules, and tissue culture grew Cryptococcus neoformans, which are diagnostic findings for Cryptococcosis.
The patient presented with a tender nodule on her forehead, which was diagnosed as Cutaneous Cryptococcosis based on the skin biopsy and tissue culture results.
The patient was treated with fingolimod for multiple sclerosis, which can cause immunodeficiency, and presented with Cryptococcosis, suggesting an immunodeficiency-associated infection.

rationales.F02: Fingolimod treatment increases the risk of opportunistic infections, including cryptococcosis.
rationales.F06: The presence of a crusted papule on the forehead is consistent with cutaneous cryptococcosis.
rationales.F10: The skin biopsy showing granulomatous inflammation and narrow-budding yeasts with thick capsules is diagnostic of cryptococcosis.
rationales.F11: The growth of Cryptococcus neoformans in tissue culture confirms the diagnosis of cryptococcosis.
rationales.F12: The negative HIV test result decreases the likelihood of immunodeficiency-associated cryptococcosis.

frontier_selector.rationale: The patient's presentation with a tender nodule on the forehead, skin biopsy showing granulomatous inflammation with narrow-budding yeasts, and tissue culture growing Cryptococcus neoformans specifically support Cutaneous Cryptococcosis, which is a subtype that fits the case evidence.
